title: Overfitting, regularisation, train and test splits
story:
A model with enough parameters can reproduce its training data exactly, including the parts of it that are accidents. That is the whole problem, and every technique here follows from it.

The distinction to hold is between structure that will recur and structure that happened. A model cannot tell them apart, because both are present in the data in exactly the same way. What separates them is not a property of the examples but a fact about the future, which no examples contain. So the only way to detect that a model has learned accidents is to check it against data it has never seen — not as good practice, but because there is no other source of the information.

Hence the split. Hold some examples back, train on the rest, and measure on the held-back portion. When performance on the training examples keeps improving while performance on the held-back ones stops improving or declines, that gap is the model learning things which do not generalise, and the gap is measurable in a way that overfitting itself is not.

The subtle failure is worth more attention than the basic idea, because almost everyone commits it. If you use the held-back set to decide anything — when to stop, which architecture, which settings — then you have optimised against it, and its estimate of future performance is no longer honest. It has become part of the training process, just with a slower and more manual feedback loop. The number it reports is now the best of everything you tried, which is a biased estimate by construction, and the bias grows with the number of things tried.

Which is why there are three portions rather than two. One to learn from, one to make decisions against, and one touched once at the end to find out what you actually have. The third is the only unbiased number available, and its value is destroyed by looking at it twice.

The techniques for reducing overfitting all work by making the model's job harder in some specific way, and it is worth seeing them as one idea. Penalising large weights makes complicated functions more expensive than simple ones, so the model prefers simplicity unless the data pays for complexity. Removing units at random during training stops any one unit from being relied upon, so the network cannot build fragile arrangements where a feature only works alongside several specific others. Stopping training early cuts it off before it has time to fit the accidents. Adding more data works directly, since accidents do not repeat and structure does.

All of them trade capacity for generalisation, and all of them can be overdone — a model prevented from fitting accidents can also be prevented from fitting the real structure, which shows up as poor performance on both portions rather than a gap between them. That symmetry is the useful diagnostic: a gap means too much capacity, and both being bad means too little, or the wrong kind.

One limitation to keep, since the split is treated as a guarantee. It only works if the held-back examples resemble what the model will actually meet. Split a time-ordered dataset at random and information from the future leaks into training, so the estimate is optimistic in a way nothing in the procedure reveals. The split has to respect whatever structure the data has — time, groups, individuals — or it measures the wrong thing confidently.

problem.name: Structure versus accident
problem.shape: A model has enough capacity to reproduce its training data, including the parts that will not recur.
tell: training performance keeps improving while held-out performance does not
the held-out set has been consulted many times

problem.move: Split into three: one portion to learn from, one to make decisions against, and one touched once at the end. Then read the pattern — a gap between training and held-out means too much capacity, and both being poor means too little or the wrong kind.
problem.invariant: Nothing in the examples distinguishes structure that recurs from structure that happened, so detecting a model that learned accidents requires data it has never seen. There is no other source of that information.
problem.breaks: The split only estimates future performance if the held-back examples resemble what the model will meet. Splitting time-ordered data at random leaks information from the future into training, producing an optimistic estimate that nothing in the procedure reveals.

cost.time: data held back is data not learned from, which is expensive when examples are scarce
cost.space: three portions to manage, and discipline about which has been touched
cost.beats: training on everything and measuring on it, which uses all the data and cannot detect the problem at all, and cross-validation, which recovers the held-back data at the cost of training several times

worked.problem: Why is a held-out set that you have consulted many times no longer a valid estimate of future performance?
worked.reasoning:
Because consulting it makes it part of the training process, with a slower and more manual feedback loop.

Start from what the set is for. Nothing in the examples distinguishes structure that will recur from structure that merely happened — both are present in the data in exactly the same way, and what separates them is a fact about the future rather than a property of the examples. So the only way to detect a model that has learned accidents is to check it against data it has never seen. That is not good practice; it is the only source of the information.

Now consider what happens when the held-out set informs a decision. You try an architecture, measure, try another, measure, pick the better one. Or you watch the held-out number during training and stop when it turns. Each of those is an optimisation step in which the held-out data supplied the signal. The model was not trained on those examples directly, but the choices around it were, and the reported number is now the best of everything you tried.

That makes it a biased estimate by construction, and the bias grows with the number of things tried — which is why it feels harmless. Each individual glance is small, nothing is obviously wrong, and the number drifts upward from honest to flattering with no point at which it visibly breaks.

Hence three portions rather than two: one to learn from, one to make decisions against, and one touched exactly once at the end. The third is the only unbiased number available, and its value is destroyed by looking at it twice — so the discipline is about access rather than about statistics.

The techniques for reducing overfitting are worth seeing as one idea while we are here: penalising large weights makes complicated functions more expensive than simple ones; removing units at random stops any one from being relied upon, so fragile arrangements cannot form; stopping early cuts training off before it fits the accidents; more data works directly, since accidents do not repeat and structure does. All trade capacity for generalisation and all can be overdone.

That gives the diagnostic worth carrying: a gap between training and held-out performance means too much capacity, and both being poor means too little capacity or the wrong kind. Those need opposite responses, and the pattern tells you which.

And the limitation, since the split gets treated as a guarantee: it only estimates future performance if the held-back examples resemble what the model will meet. Split time-ordered data at random and information from the future leaks into training, so the estimate is optimistic and nothing in the procedure reveals it. The split must respect whatever structure the data has — time, groups, individuals — or it measures the wrong thing confidently.

problem.practice: Count how many times you have looked at your held-out number while making decisions. That count is roughly how much the number is inflated, and if it is more than one, you do not currently have an unbiased estimate of anything.

beats.broke: A model with enough capacity reproduces its training data including the accidents, and nothing in the examples distinguishes an accident from structure that will recur.
beats.fix: Hold data back and measure on it, in three portions — one to learn from, one to decide against, one touched once at the end — because data never seen is the only source of that information.
beats.cost: Held-back data is data not learned from, and the final portion's value is destroyed by looking at it twice, so the discipline is about access rather than statistics.

interview.trap: Thinking the set stays valid because the model never trained on it directly. The choices around the model were trained on it, so the reported number is the best of everything you tried.
